invariants: The Dockerfile builds on the live production service: the cache mount id s/<live service id>-<target> matches Railway's documented cache-mount form.
The manual deploy workflow posts to the live production project/environment/service, not the retired project.
No application code, database, runtime variables, secrets, or data resources change.
doors: GitHub Actions railway-deploy.yml manual dispatch (workflow_dispatch) — the only door the workflow ids serve
Railway BUILD_IMAGE Dockerfile validation — the cache-mount id door
Auto-deploy on merge to main (GitHub-connected Railway binding) — unaffected: no Dockerfile cache-mount semantics change

findings.scenario: A production deployment runs after the Railway service migration while the Dockerfile cache mount and railway-deploy.yml still carry the retired project/service ids, so Railway rejects the Dockerfile at BUILD_IMAGE validation
findings.invariant: The manual Railway deployment workflow targets the live production project, environment, and service; the Dockerfile cache mount id embeds the live production service id in Railway's documented cache-mount form
findings.note: Provider-side resource migration (Railway service/account move) invalidated hard-coded deployment identifiers; fixed in this PR by re-targeting the live production resources (Dockerfile cache mount + railway-deploy.yml ids). Status registered because the production redeploy itself executes only after merge (auto-deploy on main), and the RAILWAY_TOKEN secret's access to the new project is a provider-side control the repository cannot read back — the PR body documents the distinction and the owner-gated production verification.
